title: Ani, hu, hi: pronouns
topic: נ ן; the shva; singular personal pronouns
why: The letter נ and its final form, the shva (the "almost nothing" vowel), and the pronouns I, you, he, she, to introduce yourself and someone else without the verb "to be".

New letter: נ and ן

LetterNameSound
נnunn
ןfinal nunn, at the end of a word

Like מ / ם, the letter נ has a final form, longer, that goes down below the line: ן.

לָבָןlavan: white

You already recognize ב without a dot (v): la-va-n.

", "

The shva: almost nothing

Two dots, one above the other, under a letter: that's the shva. At the start of a word, it's read as a very short e (like the a in \"about\", said very quickly); in the middle or at the end of a word, it isn't read at all.

שְׁלוֹמְךָshlomkha: the first shva is almost silent, and so is the second

Under א, you'll often see a variant: אֲ, which is read as a short a. It's the start of אֲנִי (ani, I).

The shva under וְ gives \"ve\", the little word \"and\" that attaches to the next word: וְאַתָּה? (and you?).

", "

I, you, he, she

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
אֲנִיaniI, me
אַתָּהatayou (to a man)
אַתְּatyou (to a woman)
הוּאhuhe, him
הִיאhishe

In הוּא, the vav with a dot in the middle is read \"u\" (like the oo in food): you'll see it again in the next lesson. The final א is silent.

הוּא אַבָּא, הִיא אִמָּא.He's Dad, she's Mom. [hu aba, hi ima]

Still no verb \"to be\": \"he dad, she mom\". To answer an introduction: נָעִים מְאוֹד (na'im me'od, nice to meet you).
